wine.name: Giulio Ferrari Riserva del Fondatore
wine.grapes: Chardonnay alone, a Blanc de Blancs.
wine.sites: Maso Pianizza, a vineyard of the house on the slopes above Trento at about 500 to 600 metres, the source of the first vintage in 1972.
wine.making: The base wine is made in stainless steel. The second fermentation follows in bottle, and the wine then rests close to ten years on its lees in the house's cellars before it is disgorged, with very little sugar added at the dosage.
wine.glass: Golden apple, candied citrus peel and chamomile over toast, almond paste and a chalky edge; a fine, persistent mousse, a creamy, layered texture and a long, dry finish.
wine.ageing: Ready to drink when it is released after its long rest on the lees, it keeps developing in bottle for a decade and more.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius, as the house advises; no need to decant; a tulip glass or a white wine glass rather than a narrow flute.

label.means: The collective name of the Trento DOC, the appellation for classic method sparkling wine from the province of Trento.
The founder's reserve: the house's name for its long aged wine, in honour of Giulio Ferrari.

records.table: Giulio Ferrari Riserva del Fondatore is Ferrari's Chardonnay from Maso Pianizza above Trento, fermented a second time in bottle and left close to ten years on its lees. It shows how mountain Chardonnay takes long ageing, so pour it cool in a tulip glass.
records.story: Giulio Ferrari, born in 1879 in the Trentino, then part of the Austrian Tyrol, trained at the agrarian institute of San Michele all'Adige and studied abroad, Champagne among the places he learned. Struck, as the Trentodoc institute tells it, by the likeness between the hills of Trentino and Champagne, he returned to Trento in 1902 and began to make sparkling wine by the classic method, with its second fermentation in bottle. He is credited with bringing Chardonnay to the Trento hills. In 1952, childless and in his seventies, he sold his small house to a Trento wine shop owner of the Lunelli family, who, by the house's account, went deep into debt to buy it. In 1972 the new owners set aside some five thousand bottles from the grapes of Maso Pianizza for long ageing, and in 1980, as the house tells it, they emerged as the first Giulio Ferrari Riserva del Fondatore. In 1993 Trento DOC was recognised as an appellation for classic method sparkling wine alone, by the Trentodoc institute's account the first in Italy. Open the Riserva del Fondatore when a guest asks how Italian sparkling wine ages: Chardonnay alone, from one hillside, after close to a decade on its lees.

others.name: Ferrari Perlé
others.note: A vintage Blanc de Blancs of Chardonnay, the house's middle tier between the Brut and the Riserva del Fondatore.

others.name: Ferrari Brut
others.note: The non vintage Chardonnay that carries the Trento DOC name abroad.

others.name: Ferrari Rosé
others.note: A non vintage rosé of Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.

traps: Ferrari of Trento takes its name from Giulio Ferrari and has no tie to the car maker of Maranello.
Trento DOC is in Trentino; Franciacorta, the other classic method appellation guests name, is in Lombardy.
The Riserva del Fondatore is Chardonnay alone, a Blanc de Blancs, while the house's rosé carries Pinot Noir.

cards.front: Giulio Ferrari Riserva del Fondatore: which grape, and from which vineyard?
cards.back: Chardonnay alone, from Maso Pianizza, a vineyard of the house at about 500 to 600 metres above Trento.

cards.front: Which vintage was the first Riserva del Fondatore, and in which year was it released?
cards.back: The 1972, set aside from Maso Pianizza grapes and released in 1980, as the house tells it.

questions.q: A guest asks how long Ferrari's Giulio Ferrari Riserva del Fondatore spends on its lees before it is disgorged. Which answer fits?
opts: Close to ten years
About fifteen months
About three years
Over thirty years
questions.exp: The house's technical sheets give well over nine years on the lees, close to a decade, far longer than the three years of many vintage sparkling wines.

questions.q: In 1952 the childless Giulio Ferrari sold his Trento house. To whom?
opts: A Trento wine shop owner of the Lunelli family
The Champagne house of Moët et Chandon
A cooperative of Trentino growers
The agrarian institute of San Michele all'Adige
questions.exp: He sold it to a Trento wine merchant of the Lunelli family, who went into debt to buy it; San Michele all'Adige is the agrarian institute where Ferrari trained.

sources.title: Ferrari Trento: About us, the history of the house
Ferrari Trento: Giulio Ferrari Riserva del Fondatore
Ferrari Trento: technical sheet of Giulio Ferrari Riserva del Fondatore 2004
Trentodoc: History of the Trento DOC
Glass of Bubbly: Giulio Ferrari, father of Trentodoc

report: Searches for this record: seven (the house's domain twice, the Trentodoc institute once, four open), with the house's history page, its product page and its technical sheets read through search summaries.

Giulio Ferrari's birth in 1879 rests on Wikipedia (Ferrari Trento) and Glass of Bubbly; his death in 1965 on Wikipedia alone, so the story gives only his birth year, and Bruno Lunelli's dates (1907 to 1973, Wikipedia alone) are not given, so he is described as a Trento wine shop owner of the Lunelli family.

The buyer's son who set aside the 1972 bottles is living and is not named; the first vintage 1972, released in 1980, rests on the house's history page and a merchant (Centro Bibite), and Maso Pianizza at 500 to 600 metres on several merchants.

His training at San Michele rests on the Trentodoc institute, his study in Champagne on Glass of Bubbly and Liberty Wines, and Chardonnay brought to the Trento hills on Liberty Wines and the house's own words, hedged as credited.

Dosage: the house's 1997 sheet says Extra Brut and its 2004 sheet a very small dosage, while one merchant lists the wine as Brut, so the label terms leave dosage out and the making says very little sugar.
One merchant calls Maso Pianizza Italy's first documented Chardonnay vineyard, planted in 1897, and another cites a gold medal at Milan in 1906; neither has a second source, and both are left out.
The library's p-ferrari and w-giulio-ferrari agree with the record; Ferrari Rosé in others rests on the Brennan's list bottle (Pinot Noir and Chardonnay).

wine.name: Granato
wine.classification: Indicazione Geografica Tipica, the regional tier below DOC
wine.sites: Vineyards of the house on the Campo Rotaliano, the plain of gravel and sand laid down by the Noce and the Adige: at first one old pergola vineyard, later several parcels.
wine.making: Fermented in open wooden vats with some weeks on the skins. For years part of the wine was raised in small oak barrels; later vintages are aged about fifteen months in large wooden casks, with a short time in cement before bottling.
wine.glass: Black cherry and blackberry over iron, dried herbs and a touch of violet; fresh acidity and firm, slightly rustic tannin, more savoury than lush, with a long, dark finish.
wine.ageing: Firm and closed in its first years, it opens after about five and keeps for well over a decade in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle an hour ahead; a large Bordeaux glass.

label.means: A regional IGT, wider in area and freer in its rules than the Teroldego Rotaliano DOC.
The red grape of Trentino, at home on the Campo Rotaliano, the plain north of Trento.

records.table: Granato is Foradori's Teroldego from old vines on the gravel of the Campo Rotaliano, raised in wood. Black cherry, iron and dried herbs over firm tannin show that the grape can make a red to keep, so decant it when young.
records.story: The Campo Rotaliano, the plain of gravel where the Noce meets the Adige north of Trento, is the home of Teroldego, and in 1939 the Foradori family bought a winery at Mezzolombardo on its edge. In 1984, after her father's death, the family's daughter, about twenty years old, took over the cellar. She began to propagate Teroldego by massal selection from the old vines of the estate, choosing quality over quantity, and in the late 1980s she made the first Granato, from an old pergola vineyard, raised in wood and meant to age. It showed that the grape of the plain could make a red of depth and long life. From 2002 the whole estate was farmed biodynamically, and Demeter certified it in 2009. In 2008 she began to make wine in clay amphorae, which came to shape single vineyard Teroldego such as Sgarzon, while Granato stayed in wood: small barrels in its early years, large casks later. Granato is labelled under the regional IGT rather than the Teroldego Rotaliano DOC. Pour it for a guest who has never met Teroldego: it shows what the grape of the Campo Rotaliano gives from old vines and time in wood.

others.name: Sgarzon
others.note: Teroldego from a single vineyard, aged in clay amphorae and lighter in frame than Granato.

others.name: Fontanasanta Manzoni Bianco
others.note: A white from Manzoni Bianco, a crossing of Riesling and Pinot Bianco, made with skin contact.

traps: Granato grows on the Campo Rotaliano, yet it is labelled Vigneti delle Dolomiti IGT, not Teroldego Rotaliano DOC.
Teroldego is a parent of Lagrein; both are native to Trentino and Alto Adige, and they are two grapes, not one.
The clay amphorae of Foradori shape single vineyard wines such as Sgarzon; Granato is raised in wood.

cards.front: Foradori's Granato: which grape, and from what kind of vineyard did the first one come?
cards.back: Teroldego alone, first from an old pergola vineyard on the gravel of the Campo Rotaliano.

cards.front: What did the young heir of Foradori do with Teroldego after taking over the cellar in 1984?
cards.back: She propagated it by massal selection from old vines, choosing quality over quantity, which led to the first Granato in the late 1980s.

questions.q: A guest reads Vigneti delle Dolomiti on a bottle of Foradori Granato and asks what it means. Which answer fits?
opts: A regional IGT, wider than the Teroldego Rotaliano DOC
A single walled vineyard on the Campo Rotaliano
A DOCG for the long aged reds of Trentino
The name of the estate's biodynamic certifier
questions.exp: It is the regional IGT on Granato's label, a tier below DOC and wider than the Teroldego Rotaliano DOC; it names no single vineyard.

questions.q: In which year did the Foradori family buy its winery at Mezzolombardo, on the Campo Rotaliano?
questions.exp: The family bought the winery in 1939; 1984 is the year the family's daughter took over the cellar and began the work that led to Granato.

sources.title: Quill and Pad: Foradori, exciting local grape varieties from Trentino
Foradori press archive: Wine Spectator, Scaling new heights in Italy's Dolomites

report: Searches for this record: seven (two on the house's domains, the second returning only its archive of press articles, one on four press domains, four open), so every fact rests on two secondary sources and no primary.

Granato's first vintage is 1986 in Decanter's profile, a merchant's history and a press article kept on the house's site, but 1988 in Uncorked in Italy and another Decanter article (the 1988 first bottled in 1989), so the story says the late 1980s.

The takeover is 1984 in most accounts and 1985 in one; the father's death is dated 1976 by one source and 1985 by another, so the story gives it no year; the heir and her son are living and are not named.

Biodynamics rest on Decanter (begun on part of the estate in 2000, the whole by 2002, Demeter in 2009) and Quill and Pad (2002 and 2009); amphorae from 2008 on Quill and Pad and the house's press archive.

The élevage changed: Wine Spectator and a producer sheet describe new barriques for Granato in earlier years, a German profile and merchants about fifteen months in large wooden casks later (oak in one account, acacia in two), so the making gives both without a year of change.

Founded is left empty, as in the library: one account dates the winery to 1901 and the family's purchase to 1939; the Teroldego Rotaliano DOC is dated 1971 by most and 1970 by Cavit, so no year is given for it.

The Campo Rotaliano as the gravel and sand of the Noce and the Adige rests on Cavit and two guides; the IGT on the label on vino.com, Wine Berserkers and Falstaff listings; one press article says the wine later blends five vineyards, pergola and Guyot, another three, so the sites say several parcels.

records.place: Terlano, Alto Adige Terlano DOC, Alto Adige

wine.name: Terlaner Pinot Bianco Riserva Vorberg
wine.classification: Riserva, a longer aged wine under the Alto Adige DOC rules
wine.grapes: Pinot Bianco alone, Weißburgunder in German.
wine.sites: The Vorberg, steep slopes facing south and south west above Terlano at about 450 to 650 metres, on volcanic quartz porphyry with sandy, quartz rich, slightly acid soils.
wine.making: Fermented slowly at a cool, controlled temperature in large oak casks, with malolactic fermentation by the house's notes, then aged about a year on its fine lees in large traditional casks before bottling.
wine.glass: Ripe pear, white peach and quince over chamomile, almond and a flinty, salty edge; full and creamy from the lees, yet held taut by fresh acidity, with a long finish.
wine.ageing: Tight in its first years, it opens after about five and keeps for twenty and more, gaining honey and dried herbs.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle or give it time in the glass; a white Burgundy glass.

label.means: The subzone of the Alto Adige DOC around the village, named in Italian and in German.
The German name of Pinot Bianco, which the label may print beside the Italian.
A longer aged wine under the rules of the Alto Adige DOC.
The steep porphyry hillside above Terlano that gives the grapes.

records.table: Vorberg is Cantina Terlano's Pinot Bianco Riserva from steep porphyry slopes above the village, fermented and aged in large oak casks on its lees. Pear, quince and a flinty edge over firm acidity show how long the whites of Alto Adige can keep.
records.story: In 1893 twenty four growers of Terlano, then in the Austrian Tyrol, joined forces as a cooperative to free themselves from the large landowners who ruled the wine trade, as the house tells it, and the oldest bottle in its cellar dates from that founding year. The village's vineyards climb steep slopes of volcanic quartz porphyry, and among the first wines of the cooperative was a blend of Pinot Bianco, Chardonnay and Sauvignon. From 1955 to 1993 its cellar master, convinced that the wines were not given their due, quietly set aside about five hundred bottles of every vintage. Tasted years later, they had aged with grace, and his habit of long ageing on the fine lees became the house's method. Its Rarity wines reach the market only after at least ten years in the cellar, and the archive of old vintages he began lets the house show what time does to its whites. Vorberg, the steep porphyry hillside above the village, gives the Pinot Bianco Riserva that carries the idea into every vintage: large oak casks, a year on the lees and a wine built to keep. Pour it for a guest who doubts that Pinot Bianco can age.

others.name: Terlaner I Primo Grande Cuvée
others.note: A blend, mainly Pinot Bianco with up to a third Chardonnay and some Sauvignon.

others.name: Rarity
others.note: A wine, often Pinot Bianco, released only after at least ten years maturing in the cellar.

others.name: Terlaner Cuvée
others.note: The old blend of Pinot Bianco, Chardonnay and Sauvignon, one of the house's wines since its founding.

traps: Terlaner is simply the German form of Terlano, not a grape or a style.
Rarity is no vineyard: it is a wine held at least ten years in the cellar before release.
In Alto Adige a cooperative is no lesser tier: Cantina Terlano is a cooperative of growers, and Vorberg is its Riserva.

cards.front: Cantina Terlano's Vorberg: which grape, and what rock lies beneath the slope?
cards.back: Pinot Bianco, on steep south and south west slopes of volcanic quartz porphyry above Terlano.

cards.front: What did Cantina Terlano's cellar master of 1955 to 1993 quietly do with every vintage?
cards.back: He set aside about five hundred bottles, convinced the wines could age; tasted years later, they had.

questions.q: In which vessels is Cantina Terlano's Vorberg Riserva fermented and then aged on its lees?
opts: Large oak casks
New small barriques
Clay amphorae
Glass lined concrete tanks
questions.exp: The house ferments Vorberg slowly in large oak casks and ages it about a year on its lees in large traditional casks; small new barriques would mark it with wood.

questions.q: How did Cantina Terlano begin as a winery in 1893?
opts: Twenty four growers joined as a cooperative
A Bolzano merchant bought the village vineyards
The parish priest founded a cellar for the poor
A monastery opened its cellars to the village
questions.exp: Twenty four growers founded it to free themselves from the large landowners; it was a parish priest who founded Cantina Tramin, in 1898.

sources.title: Decanter: Cantina Terlano Pinot Blanc, wines reviewed
World of Fine Wine: Cantina Terlano, Italian white wines

report: Searches for this record: four (two on the house's domain, two open), with the history, archive and Vorberg pages read through search summaries.

The cellar master of 1955 to 1993 is Sebastian Stocker on the house's archive page, in Decanter and in World of Fine Wine; his death in 2017 is in Decanter alone and his birth year in none, so he is described, not named.
One merchant (Superiore) dates his first long lees trials to 1967, in pressure tanks made for sparkling wine; with no second source that year is left out.
No source gave the first vintage of Vorberg, so the story gives none.

The plan's words Terlaner Pinot Bianco Riserva Vorberg are kept as the name; the label prints Vorberg, Pinot Bianco Riserva and Alto Adige Terlano DOC (Weißburgunder, Südtirol Terlaner in German), so the integrator may prefer the name read as the label does.
The library calls the house's grand blend Terlaner I Grande Cuvée; the house's own page names it Terlaner I Primo Grande Cuvée, as the record does.

Malolactic fermentation and casks of 70 and 30 hectolitres rest on the house's sheet for one vintage; a merchant's note of the 2015 says partly fermented in large barrels, and a guide places the slopes on the Monzoccolo, left out for want of a second source.

records.place: Tramin, Termeno in Italian, Alto Adige DOC, Alto Adige

wine.name: Gewürztraminer Nussbaumer
wine.sites: Vineyards near the Nussbaumer farm at Söll, Sella in Italian, above Tramin, about 350 to 550 metres up facing south and south east, on calcareous gravel with loam over porphyry.
wine.making: Fermented slowly at a cool, controlled temperature in small stainless steel tanks, the must settled by natural sedimentation. The wine then stays in tank on its lees until the end of the following August and rests about three months in bottle: at least fourteen months in all.
wine.glass: Lychee, rose petal and ginger over candied orange peel and clove; broad, almost oily in texture, yet dry, with fresh acidity and a long finish of bitter almond.
wine.ageing: Open and perfumed on release, it keeps and gains depth for five to ten years in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a white wine glass with a generous bowl.

label.means: The spiced Traminer, the grape whose name, by tradition, recalls the village of Tramin.
The DOC of the province of Bolzano, printed in Italian, in German or in both.
The farm near Söll whose vineyards give the wine.

records.table: Nussbaumer is Cantina Tramin's dry Gewürztraminer from vineyards at Söll above Tramin, the village said to have given the Traminer its name. Lychee, rose and ginger over a broad, oily texture stay fresh in the glass, so pour it cool beside spiced dishes.
records.story: Tramin, Termeno in Italian, is the village whose name the Traminer grape is said to carry, and by the house's account Gewürztraminer has grown on its slopes for over a thousand years. In 1898 the village's parish priest, who later sat in the Austrian parliament, founded a growers' cooperative so that small farmers could stand together through hard times. In 1971 it merged with the cooperative of Egna, Neumarkt in German, founded in 1893. Nussbaumer takes its name from a farm near Söll, the hamlet called Sella in Italian, at the foot of Mount Roen above the village, where the vineyards lie on calcareous gravel and loam over porphyry. Fermented in small steel tanks and kept on its lees until the summer after the harvest, it is the cellar's dry Gewürztraminer, as the house describes it: perfumed and broad, yet fresh. Later the cellar added Epokale, a Gewürztraminer laid down for years in a disused mine before release. Pour it when a guest asks where the grape's name began: the answer is in the glass and on the map.

others.name: Epokale Gewürztraminer
others.note: A selection laid down for years in a disused mine tunnel before release.

others.name: Stoan
others.note: The house's white blend, led by Chardonnay.

traps: The village is Termeno in Italian and Tramin in German: one place, two names.
The link between Gewürztraminer and Tramin is a naming tradition, not a settled origin of the grape.
Nussbaumer is made dry, though its perfume of lychee and rose can suggest sweetness.

cards.front: Cantina Tramin's Nussbaumer: what does the name refer to, and where?
cards.back: A farm near Söll, Sella in Italian, at the foot of Mount Roen above Tramin, whose vineyards give the wine.

cards.front: Who founded Cantina Tramin in 1898, and why?
cards.back: The parish priest of Tramin, later a member of the Austrian parliament, to help small growers through hard times.

questions.q: A guest asks whether Cantina Tramin's Nussbaumer Gewürztraminer is a sweet wine. Which answer fits?
opts: Dry, fermented in steel and kept on its lees
Sweet, from grapes dried on mats for months
Sweet, from grapes left late on the vine
Off dry, sweetened with grape must
questions.exp: The house makes Nussbaumer as a dry Gewürztraminer, fermented in small stainless steel tanks and kept on its lees until the following summer; its lychee and rose perfume only suggests sweetness.

questions.q: In 1971 Cantina Tramin merged with the cooperative of which neighbouring village?
opts: Egna, Neumarkt in German
Terlano, Terlan in German
Caldaro, Kaltern in German
Magrè, Margreid in German
questions.exp: Tramin merged in 1971 with the cooperative of Egna, founded in 1893; Terlano's cooperative, also of 1893, is a separate cellar to the north.

report: Searches for this record: five (two on the house's domain, three open), with the house's story, Gewürztraminer and Nussbaumer pages read through search summaries.

The founding priest is Christian Schrott on the house's own page and in the wein.plus glossary; Deutsche Biographie lists a priest and politician of that name, 1853 to 1936, but no second source ties those dates to Tramin, so he is described, not named.
Nussbaumer's first vintage is 1992 in one review only and is left out; Epokale's first vintage, 2009, rests on one source and is left out too.

The farm is Nussbaumerhof near Sella in Winebow, the site Sella at the foot of Mount Roen in Xtrawine and Söll in Reverse Wine Snob; the house's page gives 350 to 550 metres, south east and south, calcareous gravel with loam on porphyry, and does not name the hamlet.

The making follows the house's Nussbaumer page (small steel tanks, lees until the end of August, three months in bottle, at least fourteen months); Italian Wines gives about fifteen months with stirring and Reverse Wine Snob almost a year; no source names oak.
One merchant dates the founding to 1889; the house and the others give 1898, the library's year; the 1971 merger with Egna rests on the house and Grape Guru.
The living cellar master, in post from the early 1990s, is not named; the merger is told without the size of either cellar.

records.place: Magrè sulla Strada del Vino, Margreid in German, Alto Adige

wine.name: Löwengang Chardonnay
wine.sites: Vineyards around the Löwengang estate at Magrè, at about 230 to 330 metres, on sandy, gravelly soils rich in limestone, an alluvial fan of dolomite rock.
wine.making: Fermented with its own yeasts in barriques and larger casks, as the house describes it; the wine then stays on its lees for several months and rests about a year in bottle before release.
wine.glass: White peach, ripe pear and lemon curd over hazelnut and a little toast; creamy in texture, held by fresh acidity, with a long, saline finish of wet stone.
wine.ageing: Tight on release, it opens over three to five years and keeps for a decade and more.
wine.serve: 10 to 13 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle or give it air in the glass; a white Burgundy glass.

label.means: The manor at Magrè, bought by the family in 1934, that names the wine.
The DOC of the province of Bolzano, in Italian and in German.

records.table: Löwengang Chardonnay is Alois Lageder's barrel fermented white from the family's manor at Magrè, made with its own yeasts in barriques and larger casks and given a year in bottle before release. Peach, pear and hazelnut over fresh acidity; serve it cool, not cold.
records.story: The house traces its beginning to 1823, when the family's founder, a wagon maker in Bolzano, began to trade in wine; his successors bought vineyards and began to make wine themselves. In 1934 the family bought the Löwengang estate at Magrè, a manor of medieval origin whose name, as the house tells it, goes back to the Gaun family, raised to knights in 1674 with the title von und zu Löwengang. In the early 1980s the family set out to make a Chardonnay fermented and aged in barrel, as Burgundy does, and by the house's account the first Löwengang Chardonnay, of the 1983 vintage, reached the market in 1984. In 1995 the house moved its seat from Bolzano to Magrè, and from 2004 its own vineyards turned to biodynamic farming, with the first certified wines in 2008. Löwengang carries the estate's name and shows what the limestone rich gravel of the valley floor at Magrè gives Chardonnay when it is fermented in wood with its own yeasts and given time. For a sommelier it is the Chardonnay of Alto Adige to know by name: barrel fermented, from one estate, and made to keep.

others.name: Gaun Chardonnay
others.note: A separate Chardonnay of the house, with part of the grapes fermented whole.

others.name: Cor Römigberg
others.note: A single vineyard Cabernet Sauvignon from the warm Römigberg slope.

traps: Löwengang names the manor and more than one wine of the house; the barrel fermented white is Löwengang Chardonnay.
Gaun is a different Chardonnay of the house, not a second wine of Löwengang.
Magrè is Margreid in German: one village, two names, as everywhere in Alto Adige.

cards.front: Alois Lageder's Löwengang Chardonnay: how is it fermented and aged?
cards.back: With its own yeasts in barriques and larger casks, on its lees for several months, then about a year in bottle before release.

cards.front: When did the Lageder family buy the Löwengang estate at Magrè?
cards.back: In 1934; the house itself traces its trade in wine to 1823 in Bolzano.

questions.q: Where do the grapes of Alois Lageder's Löwengang Chardonnay grow?
opts: Around Magrè, on gravel rich in limestone
On the porphyry slopes above Terlano
On the gravel plain of the Campo Rotaliano
High in the Val Venosta near Merano
questions.exp: The vineyards lie around the Löwengang estate at Magrè, about 230 to 330 metres up on limestone rich sand and gravel; the porphyry above Terlano gives Cantina Terlano's Vorberg.

questions.q: Alois Lageder traces its beginning to 1823 in Bolzano. What did the founder do that year?
opts: Began to trade in wine
Founded a growers' cooperative
Planted the first vines at Magrè
Bought the Löwengang manor
questions.exp: A wagon maker by trade, he began to trade in wine in 1823; the family bought the Löwengang manor at Magrè only in 1934.

sources.title: Alois Lageder: Löwengang Chardonnay and Löwengang Uvaggio Storico
Blick: Lageder's Chardonnay, thirty years of Löwengang

report: Searches for this record: three (two on the house's domain, one open), with the family, history, Löwengang and biodynamics pages read through search summaries.
The founder is Johann Lageder on the house's pages, but no dates were found for him, so the story describes him as a Bolzano wagon maker of the family.

The first Löwengang Chardonnay is the 1983 vintage brought to market in 1984 on the house's pages, while Decanter calls 1984 the first official vintage after trials; the story follows the house and hedges it.
Cucine d'Italia ties the first barrel trials to a meeting with Robert Mondavi in 1981 and calls the wine the first barrel aged Chardonnay of Alto Adige; with one source each, both are left out.

The move from Bolzano to Magrè in 1995 and the biodynamic dates (from 2004, first certified wines 2008) rest on the house's own pages; the 1934 purchase on the house and on Blick, which has the purchase made by the present head's grandfather.
The present head of the house and his son are living and are never named; Alois Lageder appears only as the name of the house.
The library's Lagrein Lindenburg was not checked here and is left out of others; Gaun Chardonnay rests on the house's own page.
